title: Japan Turns to Heat-Resistant Rice as Climate Warms
paragraphs: A series of record-breaking hot summers in recent years has put Japan's rice farmers under pressure. Heat stress can affect both the quality and quantity of the rice that is harvested, and hot summers have led to rice shortages in the past — most recently in 2024 after a poor harvest the previous year.
However, the development of new varieties of rice that can produce strong harvests even in extremely hot conditions could help farmers adapt and survive.

Since the late 1990s, many regions in Japan have been developing their own varieties of heat-resistant rice. These are developed by crossbreeding existing varieties, growing them in controlled conditions — such as heated greenhouses — and then testing them in normal field conditions.
This process can take many years. For example, Natsuhime, a new variety of heat-resistant rice from Niigata prefecture, took 15 years to develop.
Now, as extreme heat waves become more common, Japanese farmers are increasingly turning to these heat-resistant rice varieties to be sure of a decent crop.

According to government data, 248,000 hectares of heat-resistant rice were planted in 2025 — that's 42,000 more hectares than in 2024. And it means that a record 18% of the rice grown in Japan in 2025 was of a heat-resistant variety. That's up from just 6% 10 years ago.
And the adoption of these new varieties isn't limited to one region — heat-resistant rice was planted in 44 out of Japan's 47 prefectures in 2025.
However, by area planted, Saga prefecture on the island of Kyushu had the highest percentage of heat-resistant rice planted — at almost 67%.

Nineteen years ago, Saga experienced heat damage to its rice crop that resulted in almost no high-grade rice being harvested. Since then, the prefecture has been making great efforts to develop new varieties.
One Saga farmer, Haruki Kawasaki, told The Guardian newspaper, "I'm just grateful that we have found something that works. And it tastes great."
